name: Estriol (oestriol, an oestrogen hormone) put in the vagina
short: Vaginal oestrogen (type unstated): more breast cancer recurrence in women on aromatase inhibitors (1 cohort). Oral estriol tied to endometrial cancer. Mostly postmenopausal; no pregnancy outcome data.
text: Estriol is an oestrogen. This entry covers estriol put in the vagina (cream, gel, pessaries, or tablets combined with Lactobacillus acidophilus); nearly all the data come from postmenopausal women, not from women of reproductive age with bacterial vaginosis. Endometrium and cancer: in a Swedish case-control study (789 endometrial cancers, 3368 controls), taking estriol by mouth for at least 5 years was associated with higher odds of endometrial cancer (odds ratio 3.0) and atypical hyperplasia (8.3), while vaginal low-potency oestrogen formulations (the abstract does not name estriol for this finding) showed only weak associations. A pooled review of 12 studies of vaginal estriol (214 women) found all 337 follow-up endometrial biopsies atrophic, and a 67-woman randomised study found no atypical hyperplasia; in a 96-woman trial, endometrial thickness rose by 0.5 mm in the first 2 weeks of daily estriol pessaries and returned to baseline on twice-weekly use. A 1998 review cautions that continuous high-dose estriol may stimulate breast and endometrial tissue. Blood levels: in 10 long-term users of vaginal estriol cream, blood estriol varied widely between women and fell within 8 hours, and the authors say more research is needed to establish safety; with low-dose estriol and lactobacillus tablets in 16 women with breast cancer taking aromatase inhibitors, blood estriol rose briefly after the first dose in 15 of 16 and was slightly raised in 8 after 4 weeks, while oestrone and oestradiol did not rise; in a report of 16 women with breast cancer on aromatase inhibitors using the same tablets, Candida colonisation rose from 2 of 14 to 7 of 16 at 2 weeks before returning to baseline. A meta-analysis in breast cancer survivors says the safety of low-dose vaginal oestrogen remains unclear, especially with aromatase inhibitors, and that concerns about cancer recurrence argue for the lowest possible concentration; in a retrospective study of 185 breast and gynaecological cancer survivors treated with vaginal estriol, vaginal DHEA or ospemifene, no significant endometrial thickening or cancer recurrence was seen over 6 months. Vaginal oestrogen in general (these two abstracts do not name the oestrogen used, so their findings are not specific to estriol; both are observational studies, which show associations, not causes): in a Danish national cohort of postmenopausal women diagnosed in 1997 to 2004 with early-stage oestrogen receptor-positive breast cancer, 1957 of the 8461 women who had used neither vaginal oestrogen nor menopausal hormone therapy before diagnosis used vaginal oestrogen after it, the risk of recurrence was not significantly raised overall (relative risk 1.08, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.32) but was raised in the subgroup also receiving aromatase inhibitors as adjuvant treatment (1.39, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.85), where the authors report a raised risk of recurrence but not of death; overall mortality was lower in users of vaginal oestrogen (hazard ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.87). In the Women's Health Initiative Observational Study (45,663 women aged 50 to 79 who did not use systemic oestrogen, median follow-up 7.2 years), among women with an intact uterus the risks of stroke, invasive breast cancer, endometrial cancer and blood clots in the lungs or legs did not differ significantly between users of vaginal oestrogen cream or tablets (self-reported) and non-users. Side effects: in a 436-woman placebo-controlled trial, adverse events were rare and similar across groups; in a 93-woman trial, side effects were minor but led 10 estriol recipients and 4 placebo recipients to stop (28% and 17%, as the abstract gives them); in the 96-woman trial, 65% of estriol pessary users reported leakage; and in a 165-woman trial, adverse events, including bleeding, were equivalent with estriol cream and an estradiol vaginal ring. In the bacterial vaginosis trial of the vaginal lactobacillus product containing oestriol, given with metronidazole (450 women aged 18 to 50, randomised to three groups), no serious adverse events occurred. In a placebo-controlled trial in 360 women with vaginal infections, including bacterial vaginosis, who were given live lactobacilli combined with low-dose oestriol (240 women) or placebo (120) after their anti-infective treatment, no serious adverse event was reported during the study treatment (lactobacilli with oestriol, or placebo); the abstract does not state the product's form or route, or the women's ages or menopausal status. Pregnancy: a review of the estriol and lactobacillus tablet describes an excellent safety profile even during pregnancy, but this is a verdict without event data, and no cited study reports pregnancy outcomes. No formal interaction data were found in the cited sources; several of them concern women taking aromatase inhibitors for breast cancer, and in the Danish cohort a raised recurrence risk was reported in the subgroup taking aromatase inhibitors.
